```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)

# Mesmos helpers de report/report_template.rmd e report/monthly_report_template.rmd
# -- ver esses ficheiros para os comentarios completos sobre cada um.
report_table <- function(x, caption = NULL, max_col_width_cm = NULL, col_widths_cm = NULL) {
  ft <- flextable::flextable(round_display(x)) |>
    flextable::theme_box() |>
    flextable::bg(part = "header", bg = "gray85") |>
    flextable::bold(part = "header") |>
    flextable::fontsize(size = 9, part = "header") |>
    flextable::fontsize(size = 9, part = "body") |>
    flextable::align(align = "center", part = "header") |>
    flextable::valign(valign = "center", part = "all") |>
    flextable::autofit()
  if (!is.null(max_col_width_cm)) ft <- cap_col_width(ft, max_col_width_cm)
  if (!is.null(col_widths_cm)) ft <- set_col_max_width(ft, col_widths_cm)
  if (!is.null(caption)) ft <- flextable::set_caption(ft, caption)
  ft
}

round_display <- function(x, digits = 2) {
  x <- as.data.frame(x)
  for (col in names(x)) {
    v <- x[[col]]
    if (!is.numeric(v) || is.integer(v)) next
    if (all(v == round(v), na.rm = TRUE)) next
    x[[col]] <- vapply(v, function(val) {
      if (is.na(val)) return(NA_character_)
      d <- digits
      while (round(val, d) == 0 && val != 0 && d < 6) d <- d + 1
      sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f"), val)
    }, character(1))
  }
  x
}

cap_col_width <- function(ft, max_width_cm = 2) {
  widths_in <- dim(ft)$widths
  capped_cm <- pmin(widths_in * 2.54, max_width_cm)
  flextable::width(ft, j = seq_along(capped_cm), width = capped_cm, unit = "cm")
}

set_col_max_width <- function(ft, widths_cm) {
  widths_in <- dim(ft)$widths
  idx <- match(names(widths_cm), ft$col_keys)
  hit <- !is.na(idx)
  if (any(hit)) {
    capped_cm <- pmin(widths_in[idx[hit]] * 2.54, unname(widths_cm[hit]))
    ft <- flextable::width(ft, j = idx[hit], width = capped_cm, unit = "cm")
  }
  ft
}

rename_display <- function(x, mapping) {
  x <- as.data.frame(x)
  idx <- match(names(mapping), names(x))
  hit <- !is.na(idx)
  names(x)[idx[hit]] <- unname(mapping)[hit]
  x
}

annex_note <- function(xlsx_name) {
  if (!is.null(xlsx_name)) {
    cat(sprintf("\n*The full table is available in the accompanying workbook: `%s`.*\n", xlsx_name))
  }
}
```

**`r params$project_ref`**

Comparison window: `r params$report_start` to `r params$report_end`

Analysis date: `r params$analysis_date`

Responsible Team: `r params$username`

Code version: `r params$code_version`

This note is descriptive and fully automated, generated end-to-end by an R code pipeline (`explore_bsh_dgy_comparison.R`). It presents metrics computed from the IdentiFlight datasets of both farms, without further interpretation, except in the concluding section.

---

# Context and Purpose

Dzhankeldy (DGY) is monitored by only `r params$n_idf_dgy` IdentiFlight (IDF) units, covering a limited subset of its `r params$n_turbines_dgy` turbines -- a monitoring history too short and too narrow, on its own, to directly support a request to restore normal (non-curtailed) operation. Bash (BSH), approximately 50 km away, shares the same avian community and the same priority species (see the list below), and has an extensive monitoring history across detections, terrain, curtailment response and topography.

This note builds an indirect, comparison-based case for DGY: where BSH shows a stable, well-characterised pattern, and DGY -- despite its limited own history -- shows a consistent pattern with BSH, that consistency itself is evidence that DGY's bird activity and risk profile is not meaningfully different from BSH's.

Three lines of evidence are presented below: (1) the weekly seasonal presence and track intensity of priority species from track data, (2) topography and the associated seasonal pattern of space use, and (3) the 2026 raptor breeding survey carried out at both farms.

Priority species considered in this comparison (union of both farms' priority lists): `r params$priority_species_compare`.

# Weekly Presence of Priority Species (Track Data)

For each priority species, presence is scored 0/1 per 7-day week over the comparison window above -- 1 if at least one track of that species was detected in that week, 0 otherwise. Week bins are anchored to the same start date in both farms (not to each farm's own start of data), so that week N refers to the same calendar dates in BSH and DGY. For each species, the BSH and DGY rows are shown one above the other, in distinct colours, so that the two farms can be compared directly on a like-for-like seasonal basis. The comparison window itself is bounded by DGY's shorter history (the intersection of both farms' available periods).

<!-- Source: plot_species_presence_heatmap(), explore_bsh_dgy_comparison.R -->
```{r species-presence-plot, fig.width=6.30, fig.height=7}
if (!is.null(params$species_presence_plot)) print(params$species_presence_plot)
```

The table below summarises, per species, the percentage of weeks in the comparison window with at least one detection in each farm -- a similar percentage between farms, for a given species, indicates a similar seasonal presence pattern despite DGY's shorter own history.

## Track Intensity per IDF Unit

For the same species as in the presence plot above, the number of distinct tracks per week is divided by the number of days in that week and by the number of IDF units of the farm (`r params$n_idf_bsh` in BSH, `r params$n_idf_dgy` in DGY), giving the mean number of tracks per day per IDF unit. This normalisation controls for the difference in the number of IDF units between the two farms. The plot below shows the weekly values as bars, one row per species and farm (BSH above DGY), on the same weekly axis as the presence plot. Each row has its own y scale starting at zero, without axis values, so that only the temporal dynamics are shown; absolute values are given in the table below.

<!-- Source: plot_species_intensity_bars(), explore_bsh_dgy_comparison.R -->

# Topography and Seasonal Space-Use Comparison

Each turbine's surrounding terrain is described from a digital elevation model (DEM) by the mean elevation and mean slope within concentric 250 m and 500 m buffers around the turbine (see `R/turbine_terrain_classification.R`). DGY has its own DEM, so these metrics are computed independently for each farm. Two views are presented: the distribution of the physical metrics of each farm, and a classification of turbines as ridge, complex or flat using the same metrics and the same thresholds in both farms. Because the thresholds are common, the proportion of each class differs between farms where their relief differs. DGY is more rugged than BSH (median mean surrounding slope of `r params$terrain_median_slope_dgy` degrees at DGY and `r params$terrain_median_slope_bsh` degrees at BSH), so terrain is not treated here as equivalent across the two farms; instead, species use is also compared within the range of slope that both farms share (see Species Use in Comparable Terrain below).

<!-- Source: terrain_metrics_summary, explore_bsh_dgy_comparison.R -->

The distribution of turbines by fixed intervals of mean surrounding slope is shown below.

```{r terrain-slope-band-table}
if (!is.null(params$terrain_slope_band_comparison)) {
  report_table(rename_display(
    params$terrain_slope_band_comparison,
    c(band = "Mean Slope Interval", N_BSH = "Turbines (BSH)", pct_BSH = "% Turbines (BSH)",
      N_DGY = "Turbines (DGY)", pct_DGY = "% Turbines (DGY)")
  ))
}
```

Turbines are then classified with a single set of thresholds applied to both farms: ridge if the ridge-proximity metric (the larger of the turbine's elevation above the mean elevation of the 250 m buffer and the elevation gain between the 250 m and 500 m buffers) is at least `r params$terrain_ridge_cutoff_m` m; otherwise complex if the mean surrounding slope is at least `r params$terrain_slope_cutoff_deg` degrees; otherwise flat. The thresholds are calibrated once on the turbines of both farms taken together and are not recalculated per farm.

<!-- Source: summarise_terrain_class_counts(), R/turbine_terrain_classification.R -->

## Terrain Classification Maps

<!-- Source: plot_turbine_terrain_map(), R/turbine_terrain_classification.R -->
```{r terrain-map-helper, include=FALSE}
# Mapas a 7 x 7 cm (2.76 in): texto e pontos reduzidos (size = 3 por omissao em
# plot_turbine_terrain_map()), legenda por baixo.
shrink_map <- function(p, title) {
  for (i in seq_along(p$layers)) {
    if (identical(p$layers[[i]]$aes_params$size, 3)) p$layers[[i]]$aes_params$size <- 1.2
  }
  p + ggplot2::labs(title = title) +
    ggplot2::theme(
      text = ggplot2::element_text(size = 6),
      plot.title = ggplot2::element_text(size = 7, face = "bold"),
      axis.text = ggplot2::element_text(size = 5),
      legend.title = ggplot2::element_text(size = 6),
      legend.text = ggplot2::element_text(size = 6),
      legend.key.size = grid::unit(0.3, "cm"),
      legend.margin = ggplot2::margin(0, 0, 0, 0)
    )
}
```

## Species Use in Comparable Terrain

To compare species use under similar orographic conditions, the analysis is repeated using only the turbines whose mean surrounding slope lies in the interval common to both farms (`r params$matched_slope_range` degrees): `r params$matched_n_turbines_bsh` turbines at BSH and `r params$matched_n_turbines_dgy` at DGY. Each track is assigned to the nearest turbine (position of its first record), and only tracks nearest to a turbine in this interval are retained. As the number of IDF units covering this subset of turbines is not available, the intensity is expressed as mean tracks per day per turbine in the interval.

# Raptor Breeding Survey (BSH and DGY)

The data in this section were extracted from the report *Breeding Raptor Nest Monitoring 2026* (Bash WPP and Dzhankeldy WPP), which covers both farms. Only the species considered in the plots above are included. Breeding outcome is the classification given in the survey report (successful, failed, not started or unknown); nest-to-turbine distances are those reported for occupied nests.

# Summary and Recommendation

The priority species monitored at DGY coincide with those monitored at BSH, which is approximately 50 km away and shares the same avian community. The same species of eagles, vultures and falcons are recorded by the IdentiFlight units of both farms, and the 2026 breeding survey records nesting of the same species groups at both sites, including Egyptian Vulture and Saker Falcon. The species composition on which the protective curtailment regime of BSH was built is therefore the same composition present at DGY.

The seasonal pattern of use is also similar between the two farms. Over the same calendar window, the weekly presence of each priority species at DGY follows the pattern observed at BSH, and the weekly track intensity per IDF unit, which controls for the difference in the number of units (`r params$n_idf_dgy` at DGY and `r params$n_idf_bsh` at BSH), shows comparable temporal dynamics for the species analysed. The relief of the two farms is not identical: DGY is more rugged than BSH (median mean surrounding slope of `r params$terrain_median_slope_dgy` and `r params$terrain_median_slope_bsh` degrees, respectively). For that reason the comparison was repeated using only the turbines in the range of slope common to both farms (`r params$matched_slope_range` degrees), where the patterns of species use remain comparable.

Taken together, these elements indicate that the bird activity patterns and the risk profile at DGY can be considered similar to those at BSH. In addition, no repeated fatalities have occurred at the same turbines at DGY, which suggests that collision risk is under control. On this basis, the evidence supports returning the DGY turbines to daytime operation, as was done at BSH, while keeping the IdentiFlight monitoring in place so that the pattern can continue to be verified.
